bio:
The operation was his, and so was the argument against the war it opened. He had studied at Harvard and served as naval attaché in Washington, had opposed the Tripartite Pact until the ultranationalist right threatened his life, and told his own prime minister that he could run wild for six months or a year and had no confidence at all in the second and third.[^agawa-1979]

The Hawaii plan follows from that estimate rather than contradicting it. If the war has to be fought and cannot be won by attrition, the only thing worth trying is a single blow at the outset that buys enough time to take what is needed and then negotiate. He forced the operation through a naval staff that did not want it, against a war plan that had spent thirty years assuming the American fleet would come west and be met in a decisive battle near home.

What the plan bought was almost exactly what he said it would. Six months later, at Midway, it ran out.[^morton-1962]

sources.note: the six-months estimate and Yamamoto's position on the war, from the standard Japanese life of him in translation. Not read at page level from this environment; nothing is quoted from it

role: Commander, First Air Fleet — the striking force
bio:
A torpedo and destroyer officer with no background in aviation, commanding the most concentrated carrier force anyone had ever assembled, on an operation he had argued against. He took it three thousand miles by the northern route in radio silence, launched on the minute the order gave, recovered the aircraft, and turned away.[^japanese-monograph-97]

The withdrawal is what he is remembered for, and the case against him is that he should have stayed and struck a third time at the fuel and the repair yard. His orders told him to leave once the second wave was away; his aircrew had been briefed for warships; and three American carriers were at sea and unlocated. Whether he was cautious or correct has been argued since the war and is set out on the historiography card, where the pack also says which of the four positions it could and could not read.

He commanded the same force at Midway six months later and lost four carriers of it in a morning.[^parshall-tully-2005]

sources.note: the passage and the order to withdraw
Nagumo and the Kidō Butai at Midway, from the Japanese records

bio:
He led the first wave in and sent the signal saying surprise had been achieved. He is also, and more importantly for this pack, the principal reason the English-language account of the day looks the way it does — and a witness who has to be handled carefully.

Interrogated in Tokyo in October 1945, he gave the US Strategic Bombing Survey round figures for the two waves that do not match the operation order, described himself as an air observer, and said nothing about urging a further attack.[^ussbs-interrogations] From 1948 he was interviewed repeatedly by Gordon Prange, and it is out of those interviews that the story of a third strike urged on *Akagi*'s bridge and refused reaches the literature. Jonathan Parshall has shown that the story moved: in 1948 Fuchida put fuel tanks last in his list of targets for a further strike, and by 1963 he had them near the top.[^parshall-2010]

He is cited in this pack as a subject and not as an authority, and that is a decision with a history: *Shattered Sword* took apart his account of Midway — the packed flight decks, the five fateful minutes — from the Japanese operational records, and found that a version the whole Western literature had absorbed was substantially his invention.[^parshall-tully-2005]

sources.note: Nav. No. 6, USSBS No. 40, Tokyo, 18 October 1945

bio:
Five midget submarines were launched off Oahu before dawn and none of them came back. Sakamaki's gyrocompass failed, he grounded twice, could fire neither torpedo, and was washed ashore unconscious at Waimanalo the next morning.

He was the first Japanese prisoner of war taken by the United States, in a navy that had been taught that capture was not survivable as a matter of honour. That fact — one man, numbered first on a list that would eventually be very long — is the reason he is in this cast: the war the operation opened would be fought on both sides by people who had been told there was no such thing as surrender, and the counting starts here.[^morton-1962]

sources.note: ch. VI — the five midget submarines, all lost. The details of Sakamaki's own boat are from the shared Person entry rather than from a work this pack has opened, and the pack gives no times or positions for it

role: Commander in Chief, United States Pacific Fleet
bio:
His fleet was in port on a Sunday morning because that was where fleets were on Sunday mornings, and because the war everybody expected was going to start somewhere else — in the Philippines, in Malaya, in the Dutch islands with the oil in them. Every plan on his desk was about a Japanese move southward.

He commanded one half of an arrangement with nothing above it in Hawaii. The ships were his; the island, its aircraft, its guns and its radar were the Army's. The radar plot that saw the first wave an hour out went to an Army information centre.[^craven-cate-aaf-1] Nothing about that division was his invention and nothing about it worked.

He was relieved ten days later, reduced to rear admiral, and spent the rest of his life arguing that Washington had known more than it told him. The inquiries into 7 December have run, on and off, for eighty years, and the question of what he should have been told has not been closed by any of them.[^morton-1962]

sources.note: ch. 6 — the Opana plot and the information centre
ch. VI — the fleet in port and the expectation of a move southward

bio:
The other half of the divided command. The Army's aircraft, anti-aircraft guns and aircraft warning service on Oahu were his, and the mobile radar sets on the island were being run, on the morning of 7 December, largely as a training exercise: the plot that came in from Opana at 0702 was handled by an officer who was there “solely for training and observation” and who knew a flight of B-17s was due in from the mainland.[^craven-cate-aaf-1]

Ninety-six Army aircraft were lost that day, a great many of them on the ground.[^morton-1962] He was relieved with Kimmel, and shares with him both the blame of the first inquiry and the long argument about whether the two of them were failures or the men chosen to carry a failure that ran a good deal further up.

bio:
A mess attendant on one of the battleships that sank at its moorings — the rating the Navy reserved for Black sailors, who were not permitted to hold a gunnery rate and were not trained on the guns. On the morning of 7 December he carried wounded men clear, helped move his mortally wounded captain, and then fired an anti-aircraft gun he had never been trained on until the ammunition ran out.

He is in this cast because the day is usually counted in ships, and one of the eight battleships in the count is the one he was standing on. Nimitz pinned the Navy Cross on him aboard *Enterprise* in May 1942, the first to a Black sailor. He was still a cook when the escort carrier he had been transferred to was torpedoed off Makin in November 1943, and he went down with her.[^morton-1962]

sources.note: ch. VI — the battleships sunk at their moorings. The account of Miller's own morning is from the shared Person entry, which rests on source:toll-2011; this pack could not open that volume and gives no page

bio:
The Washington clock in this pack is very largely his diary. He had been talking to the Japanese ambassador since March; on 26 November he handed him an outline of terms whose third numbered step was the withdrawal of all Japanese forces from China and Indochina.[^peace-and-war-1943] It was a statement of a position rather than an ultimatum, and it was read in Tokyo as the end of the road — although the striking force had sailed the day before, Washington time, so it cannot have been what set the operation going.

On 7 December the ambassador asked to see him at one o'clock, put it back, and arrived at five past two. Hull read the document, asked whether it was presented on instructions, was told that it was, and then said that in fifty years of public service he had never seen a paper “more crowded with infamous falsehoods and distortions”. The two envoys left without saying anything.[^peace-and-war-1943]

sources.note: docs. 257 and 265, both read in full; the quoted words are verbatim from doc. 265

role: Ambassador of Japan to the United States
bio:
A retired admiral rather than a diplomat, sent to Washington in February 1941 because he knew the President and might be believed. He negotiated for nine months and was not told what his own government had decided.

On 7 December he was instructed to hand over a memorandum breaking off the talks at one o'clock in the afternoon. His embassy could not decode and type it by then. He asked for one o'clock, put the appointment back to a quarter to two, arrived at five past two and was received at twenty past — and when the Secretary of State asked why one o'clock in particular, said that he did not know, that was his instruction.[^peace-and-war-1943]

By then the first wave had been over Oahu for fifty-five minutes.

sources.note: doc. 265 — every one of those times, and the ambassador's own explanation, as the Secretary's memorandum of the conversation records them

role: Commander in Chief, Pacific Fleet, from 31 December 1941
bio:
He is in this cast for what comes after it. He took the Pacific Fleet at the end of December, three weeks after its battle line had been sunk at its moorings, and had to fight with what the attack had not touched: three carriers that had been at sea on the morning of the 7th, a submarine force, and a base at Pearl Harbor whose fuel, dry docks and repair shops were undamaged.[^morton-1962]

That last item is the whole of the third-wave argument in one sentence, and Nimitz is usually quoted on the other side of it — the remark that destroying the oil would have prolonged the war by two years comes down through Layton, who was his fleet intelligence officer. This pack could not open Layton and does not put the remark in quotation marks.

role: Radioman third class, Patrol Wing TWO, aged twenty
bio:
John Charles Tashner Jr. was born in Jersey City on 18 December 1920 and raised in Lynchburg, Virginia, by a mother who had left his father when the boy was three. Everyone called him Jay. In October 1938, two months short of his eighteenth birthday and fresh out of high school, he walked into the Naval Training Station at Norfolk and joined a Navy still at peace.[^tashner-family-2026][^tashner-service-record] He learned the fleet from the bottom: deck force on the ammunition ship *Nitro*, then two years in the destroyer *Selfridge* (DD-357), where he worked his way off the deck and into the radio gang — radio striker, underwater sound operator, a watchstander on the Pacific Fleet's circuits.[^tashner-service-record]

In July 1941 he made the move that shaped everything after. He left the destroyer for naval aviation, qualified in PBY flying boats with Patrol Squadron 23 at Pearl Harbor, and in November joined Commander, Patrol Wing TWO — the shore command whose long-range patrol planes were the fleet's eyes — keeping watch on the radio circuits that tied Oahu to its outlying islands and its aircraft.[^tashner-service-record] So on the morning of 7 December 1941 he was ashore, twenty years old, shaving in his skivvies when the planes came over. At the barracks door somebody pushed a rifle at him and told him to go shoot at them; the ammunition, it turned out, was locked in another building for safekeeping. Mustered and re-mustered while rumours of a landing ran through the base, he spent that day, and days after it, out on the oil-black water of the harbour, recovering the dead. He was the quiet type, typical of his generation. In all the years that followed he spoke of that morning to his eldest son exactly once.[^tashner-family-2026][^tashner-john-2026]

Six months later the war handed him a strange coda to that morning. Rated up to radioman second class, he joined the seaplane tender *Ballard* and stood radio watches through the Battle of Midway and the long search of the battle area that followed.[^tashner-service-record] On 19 June 1942, directed to a drifting open boat a PBY had spotted hundreds of miles from Midway, *Ballard* took aboard the engineering force of the sunken carrier *Hiryū* — “thirty-five Japanese navymen”, in the Naval Historical Center's account, “left for dead when she was abandoned before dawn on 5 June”. Navy photographers caught the prisoners on *Ballard*'s deck and under guard ashore at Midway; Jay's service record credits him with participating in their capture — thirty-six officers and men, by the sheet's count.[^nhc-midway-rescue][^tashner-service-record] The twenty-one-year-old who had pulled Pearl Harbor's dead out of the water ended the battle's story pulling the enemy's living out of it.

By then he was aviation to the bone. Through 1943 he taught radio in the air out of San Diego — an in-flight instructor in PBY and PB2Y-3 flying boats, flying radio in the new PB4Y-2 patrol bombers — and was designated a combat aircrewman, the winged rating he wears in his portrait. He married Margaret that year; a 1943 city directory finds the couple at 3724 Van Dyke Avenue.[^tashner-service-record][^tashner-john-2026][^tashner-family-research-2026] Then the Central Pacific offensive picked him up and carried him west. With Carrier Aircraft Service Unit 16 his record states it flatly: “Made invasion landing on Tarawa.” On Betio — the island whose airfield the November 1943 assault had been fought for — he ran a maintenance crew detachment, patching up Navy PB4Y-2s and Army B-24s. By mid-1944 he was a chief radioman at Majuro, the fleet's vast new forward anchorage, running the electronics division of the plane pool that readied replacement aircraft for the carriers; the commendations came that June and August, two of them, over the area commander's signature.[^tashner-service-record]

Somewhere in those years the Navy offered to make him an officer, and he said no. His sons remember his reasons differently, and both versions sound like him. One heard that a commission meant destroyers, and destroyers were being sunk, and he had a wife at home.[^tashner-family-2026] The other heard his father's cooler arithmetic: newly commissioned men were being fed into the slots in direct contact with the Japanese, and after the last war it was the officers who had been dismissed at the armistice while the Navy kept its enlisted technical men. The eldest also suspected — his own guess, he was careful to say, not his father's word — that his father was quietly declining his mother's ambitions for him.[^tashner-john-2026] He stayed a chief, and the Navy kept him, exactly as he had calculated. After the war his trade ran ahead into the electronic age and he ran with it: radio material school in Dearborn, electronics shops at Alameda and Norfolk, leading radio chief of TBM squadrons, and by 1950–51 flying in TBM-3W radar aircraft with anti-submarine squadron VS-22 as an airborne early warning and ASW operator-technician — one of the enlisted men working the first generation of airborne radar. Along the way, the sailor who had left high school for the fleet passed his college-level GED and scored a 3.91 on a Navy correspondence course in elementary nuclear physics.[^tashner-service-record] He wore Combat Aircrew Wings with two stars above his Pacific ribbons, retired in 1958 as a chief petty officer with four children to raise, and died in September 1977, at fifty-six.[^tashner-service-record][^tashner-family-2026][^tashner-family-research-2026] His account of the morning the war began, as his sons tell it, is the one participant voice this pack holds.
